summary: Malta is part of the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities can stay 90 days in any 180-day period (with ETIAS being phased in), and everyone else needs a €90 Schengen short-stay visa handled through Malta's Central Visa Unit and its visa centres abroad.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

source.name: European Commission — Schengen short-stay calculator (DG Migration and Home Affairs)

fee.notes: Children 6–11: €45; under 6: free. Fee set EU-wide since 11 June 2024.

For stays over 90 days: work, study and other long-stay purposes, usually alongside a residence-permit application. Confirm the current fee and requirements with Identità or the Maltese mission before applying.

passportValidity.text: Non-EU passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the last 10 years.

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000, valid across the Schengen Area for the whole stay. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it but border officers may ask about cover.

onwardTicket.text: Border officers may ask non-EU visitors for proof of return or onward travel and accommodation details.

proofOfFunds.text: Malta's commonly used reference is around €48 per person per day for the stay; border officers assess sufficiency case by case alongside accommodation and return bookings. Confirm the current guideline with the Maltese authorities.

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travellers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders. Registration happens at the border — there is nothing to submit in advance, but allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorisation System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travellers will need an ETIAS travel authorisation to enter the Schengen Area. It is being phased in — check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared when entering or leaving the EU.

notes: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 litre of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air/sea).
No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.

payments.text: Cards are widely accepted, but keep some euro cash for bus fares bought on board, small kiosks, market stalls and village festas.

safety.text: Malta is very safe with low violent crime. Watch for pickpocketing in Valletta and on crowded buses, and take the usual care in the Paceville nightlife district late at night.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Malta Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: April–June and September–October offer warm weather without the peak-summer heat and crowds; the sea stays swimmable into late October. July and August are hot, busy and expensive.

tips.text: Traffic drives on the left, British-style, and roads are narrow and busy — look right first as a pedestrian, and consider the frequent buses over hiring a car around Valletta.
Tap water is safe to drink but desalinated and often unpalatable — most visitors stick to bottled or filtered water.
The Gozo ferry from Ċirkewwa runs around the clock and you only pay on the return leg from Gozo; the fast ferry from Valletta is an alternative in season.
July and August regularly top 30°C with strong sun and big crowds at the Blue Lagoon and beaches — book accommodation early and plan sightseeing for mornings.
Apply for ETIAS only at the official travel-europe.europa.eu site once it becomes mandatory — unofficial sites charge inflated fees.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Malta?
faq.answer: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely. US, UK, Canadian, Japanese and around 60 other visa-exempt nationalities can stay up to 90 days in any 180-day period across the Schengen Area (with ETIAS being phased in). Everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa, handled by Malta's Central Visa Unit through its missions and visa centres.

faq.question: How much does a Malta Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: The Schengen short-stay visa costs €90 for adults and €45 for children aged 6–11, allowing up to 90 days in any 180-day period across all Schengen countries. National long-stay (Type D) visas cost around €100 — confirm with the Maltese mission.

faq.question: Is ETIAS required to enter Malta?
faq.answer: ETIAS is being phased in for visa-exempt travellers across the Schengen Area. During the transition, travellers without ETIAS are still admitted; once fully mandatory, the €20 online authorisation will be required before boarding. Check the official EU website for the current status.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Malta without a visa?
faq.answer: Visa-exempt non-EU visitors can stay up to 90 days within any 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area — so time spent in Italy or any other Schengen country counts toward the same limit. EU and EFTA citizens can stay indefinitely but should register if settling for more than 3 months.

faq.question: Do Gozo and Comino need separate arrangements?
faq.answer: No — Gozo and Comino are part of Malta, so whatever lets you enter Malta covers the whole archipelago. Ferries between the islands are domestic with no passport checks.
